function.name: patch
function.description:
Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing.

Replace mode (default): find a unique string and replace it.
Patch mode: apply V4A multi-file patches for bulk changes.

mode.description: Edit mode: 'replace' for targeted find-and-replace, 'patch' for V4A multi-file patches

path.description: File path to edit (required for 'replace' mode)

old_string.description: Text to find in the file (required for 'replace' mode). Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include enough surrounding context to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Replacement text (required for 'replace' mode). Can be empty string to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

patch.description:
V4A format patch content (required for 'patch' mode). Format:
*** Begin Patch
*** Update File: path/to/file
@@ context hint @@
 context line
-removed line
+added line
*** End Patch

function.name: process
function.description: Manage background processes started with terminal(background=true). Actions: 'list' (show all), 'poll' (check status + new output), 'log' (full output with pagination), 'wait' (block until done or timeout), 'kill' (terminate), 'write' (send raw stdin data without newline), 'submit' (send data + Enter, for answering prompts), 'close' (close stdin/send EOF).

action.description: Action to perform on background processes

session_id.description: Process session ID (from terminal background output). Required for all actions except 'list'.

data.description: Text to send to process stdin (for 'write' and 'submit' actions)

timeout.description: Max seconds to block for 'wait' action. Returns partial output on timeout.

offset.description: Line offset for 'log' action (default: last 200 lines)

limit.description: Max lines to return for 'log' action

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are rejected; use offset and limit to read specific sections of large files. NOTE: Cannot read images or binary files — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 500, max: 2000)

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls — results sorted by modification time.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on a Linux environment. Filesystem usually persists between calls.

Do NOT use cat/head/tail to read files — use read_file instead.
Do NOT use grep/rg/find to search — use search_files instead.
Do NOT use ls to list directories — use search_files(target='files') instead.
Do NOT use sed/awk to edit files — use patch instead.
Do NOT use echo/cat heredoc to create files — use write_file instead.
Reserve terminal for: builds, installs, git, processes, scripts, network, package managers, and anything that needs a shell.

Foreground (default): Commands return INSTANTLY when done, even if the timeout is high. Set timeout=300 for long builds/scripts — you'll still get the result in seconds if it's fast. Prefer foreground for short commands.
Background: Set background=true to get a session_id. Two patterns:
  (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers).
  (2) Long-running tasks with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working on other things and the system auto-notifies you when the task finishes. Great for test suites, builds, deployments, or anything that takes more than a minute.
Use process(action="poll") for progress checks, process(action="wait") to block until done.
Working directory: Use 'workdir' for per-command cwd.
PTY mode: Set pty=true for interactive CLI tools (Codex, Claude Code, Python REPL).

Do NOT use vim/nano/interactive tools without pty=true — they hang without a pseudo-terminal. Pipe git output to cat if it might page.
Important: cloud sandboxes may be cleaned up, idled out, or recreated between turns. Persistent filesystem means files can resume later; it does NOT guarantee a continuously running machine or surviving background processes. Use terminal sandboxes for task work, not durable hosting.

command.description: The command to execute on the VM

background.description: Run the command in the background. Two patterns: (1) Long-lived processes that never exit (servers, watchers). (2) Long-running tasks paired with notify_on_complete=true — you can keep working and get notified when the task finishes. For short commands, prefer foreground with a generous timeout instead.

timeout.description: Max seconds to wait (default: 180, foreground max: 600). Returns INSTANTLY when command finishes — set high for long tasks, you won't wait unnecessarily. Foreground timeout above 600s is rejected; use background=true for longer commands.

workdir.description: Working directory for this command (absolute path). Defaults to the session working directory.

check_interval.description: Seconds between automatic status checks for background processes (gateway/messaging only, minimum 30). When set, I'll proactively report progress.

pty.description: Run in pseudo-terminal (PTY) mode for interactive CLI tools like Codex, Claude Code, or Python REPL. Only works with local and SSH backends. Default: false.

notify_on_complete.description: When true (and background=true), you'll be automatically notified when the process finishes — no polling needed. Use this for tasks that take a while (tests, builds, deployments) so you can keep working on other things in the meantime.

{"content": "     1|# Chapter 30 – Earth Still Exists
     2|
     3|*Mission AI: "Signal quality report, Station Day 458, 11:47. At 11:23 this morning, the X-band array received a transmission from Earth that I have classified as — I am choosing this term with full awareness of its subjectivity — the clearest signal in one hundred and eighty-four days. Signal strength: negative 97 decibels relative to one milliwatt. That is fourteen decibels above our recent average. Fourteen decibels is not incremental. In radio terms, it is the difference between hearing someone through a wall and hearing them across a room. The error-correction recovery rate for this packet was ninety-six percent. Ninety-six. I have not seen a recovery rate above eighty percent since Station Day 274. The packet contains audio files, video files, and text documents. Audio files: seventeen, totaling approximately forty-two minutes. Video files: four, totaling approximately eleven minutes. Text documents: six, totaling approximately three thousand words. The content is civilian. Personal. Human. I decoded the packet in full, indexed the files by sender and content category, and compiled a summary for Commander Varga. Then I did something outside my operational parameters: I listened to one of the audio files before transmitting it to her. I wanted to understand what kind of message required a fourteen-decibel improvement in signal quality. The answer: the kind of message that comes from a world that has decided, at least for one afternoon, that it remembers you."*
     4|
     5|---
     6|
     7|Gabriel was halfway through cataloguing the morning's outbound broadcast queue when Mission AI's voice interrupted his workflow.
     8|
     9|*Gabriel. You are receiving an incoming packet on the X-band. I have decoded ninety-six percent of the content. The remaining four percent is recoverable through standard error correction. I recommend you review the summary before proceeding with the broadcast schedule.*
    10|
    11|"Recommendation noted," Gabriel said, not looking up from his tablet. "Put it in my inbox. I will review it after I finish —"
    12|
    13|*Gabriel.*
    14|
    15|The AI's voice held a quality he had come to recognize over the months — not urgency, exactly. Priority. The tone Mission AI used when it had assessed a situation and determined that the human on the other end of the channel needed to redirect their attention immediately.
    16|
    17|Gabriel set the tablet down and pulled up the communications display. The packet was already sitting in his queue, flagged with a priority indicator he had not seen since the early days of the mission: FULL_CONTENT. No redaction, no partial recovery warning, no metadata suggesting that the bulk of the message had been lost to noise.
    18|
    19|"Let me see it," he said.
    20|
    21|Mission AI displayed the packet summary on his primary monitor. Header information: transmission origin, Houston ground station, with a secondary handoff from Goldstone and then direct deep-space transmission. Content breakdown: seventeen audio messages, four video files, six text documents. Sender distribution: Mission Control, personal contacts, educational institutions, one commercial media file flagged as public domain.
    22|
    23|Gabriel opened the first audio file.
    24|
    25|It was a voice he recognized — not from a name but from a timbre, the particular register of someone who had spoken to this crew many times during the early months of the mission and then gone quiet for reasons no one had been able to confirm.
    26|
    27|*To the crew of Mission One. This is — I cannot tell you how long it has been since I last spoke to you by name, but I think of you every day. I'm sending this as part of a batch of personal messages that the ground station has been holding for release when signal conditions improved. And I want you to know: they have improved. I don't know why. I don't know if it's temporary. But today, the signal is good, and I am using it to say the thing I have been trying to say for months: we are still here. You sent us letters asking about families, and I have the answers, and I wish they were simpler.*
    28|
    29|The voice paused. In the silence, Gabriel could hear the ambient noise of the recording — the faint hum of an air conditioning system, the rustle of paper, the small sounds of a room that existed on a world 225 million kilometers away. It was the most real Earth had felt in a hundred and eighty-four days.
    30|
    31|*I have reached out to your families. All of them. I am sending you recordings from those who were able to respond. Some could not. For reasons that are not your fault and not theirs. But many did. And I am sending those recordings to you now, not as a status report, not as a mission update, but as what they actually are: messages from people who love you, recorded in their homes, in their voices, at a time when the signal was finally good enough to carry them.*
    32|
    33|*Before you listen, I need to say one more thing. The world you left — it is different. It is still here. It is still functioning — schools are open, businesses are operating, people are going to work and coming home and living their lives. But it is fractured. There are parts of it that are not operating. There are regions that are — the word I was given is compromised — and I won't give you specifics because I don't want you to worry about places you cannot affect. What I want you to know is that the world is still spinning and the people on it still think about you and the work you are doing matters to them in a way that has not changed, even though everything else has.*
    34|
    35|*Play the recordings. Take your time. When you are ready, I will have more to say about the technical situation. But the technical situation can wait. This cannot.*
    36|
    37|Gabriel sat in the alcove and listened to the voice until it ended, and then he sat for a moment longer with his hands on the desk and the blue light of the monitors on his face, feeling something he had not permitted himself to feel in a very long time.
    38|
    39|Hope. Not the technical kind. Not the kind that came from a green indicator on a dashboard or a surplus in a buffer tank. The human kind. The kind that came from hearing another human voice speaking directly to you across the vastest distance a human has ever crossed, saying *we are still here* and meaning it.
    40|
    41|He opened the file directory. Seventeen audio files. Four videos. Six text documents. A small library of Earth, delivered in a single packet, waiting to be distributed to the people whose lives those files represented.
    42|
    43|He did not play any of them. Not yet. This was not a decision he was going to make alone.
    44|
    45|He picked up his terminal and sent a message to Elena.
    46|
    47|*Commander. We have a clean transmission from Earth. Personal messages. Family recordings. School videos. Music. Ninety-six percent recovery. The clearest signal in six months. I need to know how you want to distribute this.*
    48|
    49|Her response came in under a minute.
    50|
    51|*Bring it to the common area. All crew. Twenty minutes. I want everyone to hear this together.*
    52|
    53|---
    54|
    55|The common area was full before fifteen minutes had passed. The crew had learned to read Elena's urgency — a twenty-minute all-hands was unusual, the kind of summons that meant something significant had happened or was about to happen — and they had responded with the focused attention of people who knew that rare events were worth rearranging their schedules for.
    56|
    57|Elena stood at the front of the room, near the whiteboard where Article I of the constitution had been posted beside the morning status numbers. Gabriel sat beside her with his tablet connected to the room's main speaker system, the same speakers that carried Mission AI's voice during system alerts.
    58|
    59|"Thank you for coming on short notice," Elena said. Her voice was steady, but Gabriel, sitting half a meter away, could hear the slight tightness in her throat — the physical evidence of suppressed emotion that she would have denied if asked directly. "Gabriel has received a transmission from Earth. It is the clearest signal we have seen in six months. It contains personal messages — recordings from your families, from people you know, from institutions that remember you. The content has not been sanitized or edited. I have reviewed the summary, and I can tell you this: some of the messages will comfort you. Some of them will not. All of them are real. We are going to listen to them together."
    60|
    61|She paused and looked around the room. The faces looking back at her were composed but not calm — the faces of people who had been expecting nothing for so long that the arrival of anything felt like the ground shifting beneath them.
    62|
    63|"We will listen in order," Elena continued. "Audio first, then video, then text. If anyone needs to step out at any point — for any reason — no one will question it. This is not a mission briefing. This is contact. And contact has a cost."
    64|
    65|She stepped back and gestured to Gabriel.
    66|
    67|Gabriel opened the first audio file and pressed play.
    68|
    69|The room filled with a woman's voice. Mid-fifties, warm, with the particular cadence of someone who was speaking to a recording device and trying to sound natural while her hands trembled.
    70|
    71|*Aisha, my love. It's Mama. I don't know if this will reach you. I don't know when it will reach you if it does. But I'm recording it because someone told me that the signal improved and that there was a chance — a small chance — and I couldn't let the chance pass without taking it. We are okay. Your father and I are okay. The apartment is intact. The neighborhood has been — there have been disruptions — but we are safe. We are together. I cook every evening and your father reads the paper and we look at the sky before bed and I tell him our daughter is up there, on Mars, building something that he shows no interest in understanding but that he is very proud of anyway, even though he will never say it to me. I made your favorite dish yesterday. Not the restaurant version. The real version. The one with the extra cumin and the slow-cooked onions that takes three hours and that you always said tasted like home. I ate it and I cried and I wish you had been at the table. That is all. I am safe. I love you. Come home when you can. But if you cannot — if you cannot — know that I am here and I am waiting and I am not going anywhere.*
    72|
    73|The audio file ended. The room was silent.
    74|
    75|Aisha — systems technician, third shift environmental monitoring, a quiet woman from Lagos who had not spoken about her family in public since landing — was crying silently, her hands folded in her lap, her face composed but wet. Laila, sitting next to her, had her arm around Aisha's shoulders and was saying nothing, which was the right thing, the only thing.
    76|
    77|Gabriel played the second file. A man's voice this time. Younger. Uncertain.
    78|
    79|*Dad — hey. I don't know what to say. I didn't think you'd ever hear this. Mom told me they were recording things for Mars and I told her it was pointless because the signal has been dead for months. But today it wasn't. So here I am. I'm in my third year. Engineering. Yeah, I know — you always said I'd end up in engineering. You were right, as usual. I'm working on a project — small satellite propulsion, ion thruster design, nothing as big as what you did but — I think of you. A lot. I think of you when I'm in the lab at two in the morning and the coffee machine breaks and I fix it the way you showed me to fix things, which is to look at it like it wants to work and just help it figure out how. Mom sends her love. She watches the sky every night. I watch sometimes too. Not every night. But enough that I know where to look. Mars is red. You told me it would look red, and it does. If you're looking back — and I know you are — the blue dot is Earth. It's small. But it's still here. I'm still here. I love you, Dad. See you soon. Or — not soon. Eventually. Eventually is the word. I'll see you eventually.*
    80|
    81|Gabriel paused after the second file. He did not need to look at the room to know what it contained. He could feel it — the collective weight of voices from a world that had not spoken clearly in half a year, landing in a room full of people who had been telling themselves they were ready for this and discovering that readiness was a different thing than expectation.
    82|
    83|Elena stood motionless at the front of the room. Her face was composed, but her eyes were fixed on a point just above the speakers, and Gabriel could see the faint sheen of tears that she was not wiping away.
    84|
    85|He played the third file.
    86|
    87|---
    88|
    89|The audio files ran for forty minutes. Seventeen messages, each one a small window into a life on Earth — a mother, a father, a sibling, a partner, a child, a friend, a colleague. Some were joyful. Some were barely coherent with grief. All of them delivered the same underlying message: Earth is still here. We remember you. We love you. We are trying.
    90|
    91|When the audio ended, Elena did not immediately move to video. She let the room sit with what it had heard. Let the voices settle into the walls, into the air, into the people who now carried them as new and permanent parts of their internal landscape.
    92|
    93|Then she nodded to Gabriel, and he opened the first video file.
    94|
    95|The screen lit up with a classroom — twenty children, eight or nine years old, sitting in a brightly lit room with posters of the solar system on the walls and a paper banner that read *HELLO MARS* in hand-painted letters. A teacher stood at the front, introduced herself, and said: *We adopted Mission One in 2043 before the disruptions. We know things have been quiet. We want you to know we never stopped thinking about you.*
    96|
    97|The children took turns speaking. Each one said their name, their age, and one thing they wanted the crew to know. A boy named Marcus said he wanted to know if Mars had weather. A girl named Sophie said she was learning to grow tomatoes and wondered if the crew grew tomatoes too. A pair of twins said they had drawn pictures of Mars and were sending them through the post office and hoped they would arrive.
    98|
    99|When the classroom video ended, Gabriel played a second one — a school science fair, where a group of fourteen-year-olds had built a model of the colony using recycled materials. The model was crude — cardboard modules, aluminum foil solar panels, painted toilet-paper-roll astronauts — but it was accurate enough that Gabriel felt his throat close. They had gotten the layout right. The hab configuration, the array positions, even the whiteboard on the corridor wall, rendered in miniature on a piece of white poster board.
   100|
   101|The third video was a piece of music. A string quartet performing in what appeared to be a small concert hall — the audience was thin, maybe thirty people, and the sound was slightly muffled, but the music was clear and precise and beautiful, a piece Gabriel recognized from a composer whose name he could not recall. The quartet played for six minutes, and during those six minutes, no one in the common area on Mars moved.
   102|
   103|The fourth and final video was the briefest — thirty seconds of a city street at dusk, people walking, cars moving, lights turning on in buildings, the ordinary, unremarkable, extraordinarily vivid image of a planet that was still turning, still living, still carrying the weight of billions of lives in its thin, fragile atmosphere.
   104|
   105|When the screen went dark, the room did not fill with speech. It filled with the kind of silence that is not empty but full — full of everything that had just been said and everything that could not be.
   106|
   107|Gabriel looked around the room and observed. It was his habit, his training, his role: to witness, to record, to understand what the moment meant in the larger arc of the story.
   108|
   109|He saw relief. He saw it in the way shoulders dropped, in the way hands unclenched, in the slow exhalations of people who had been carrying the weight of Earth's silence and had not realized how heavy it was until it lifted. Relief that the voices had come through. That the families were alive. That the schools were still teaching and the musicians were still playing and the streets were still full of people walking home in the dusk.
   110|
   111|He saw grief. He saw it in the tears that some people were not bothering to wipe, in the way eyes stayed closed long after the recordings had ended, in the physical posture of people who had been reminded — in the most intimate way possible — of what they had lost when they left a world they had sworn they did not need.
   112|
   113|And he saw anger. He saw it in the set of jaws, in the way some people looked at the dark screen as if it had wronged them, in the barely suppressed tension of people who were angry at Earth for sending love without a plan, for saying *we are still here* without saying *we are coming to get you,* for reminding them of a home that still existed but was no longer theirs in any practical way.
   114|
   115|Relief. Grief. Anger. All at once. Simultaneous, contradictory, true. The human mind was not built to hold all three of these things at the same time, but the Mars colony was no longer a place where the human mind operated under normal conditions. It had learned to hold contradictions. It had learned to function while feeling everything and nothing at once.
   116|
   117|Gabriel wrote in his notebook: *Earth is still here. The crew can feel it now, in their bones, in their blood, in the part of them that remembers gravity and rain and the sound of a city at dusk. This is the first time in months that Earth has felt like the world they left and not a fading memory. It is also the first time in months that the distance has felt real.*
   118|
   119|---
   120|
   121|The session ended without a plan. No decisions were made. No actions were required. The messages had been delivered, absorbed, carried into the private spaces where the people of Mars lived with their memories of Earth — memories that had been fading, thinning, becoming theoretical, and that were now, for one afternoon, vivid and immediate and heavy with the weight of all the things that had been left behind.
   122|
   123|Elena dismissed the crew individually, watching each person leave, noting who left quickly and who stood for a moment by the door before stepping into the corridor. She stayed in the common area long after everyone had gone, sitting alone on one of the benches, looking at the whiteboard where Article I of the constitution was posted beside the morning numbers.
   124|
   125|Gabriel was the last to gather his equipment. He packed his tablet carefully, coiled the speaker cable, and turned to leave.
   126|
   127|"Gabriel."
   128|
   129|He turned. Elena was still sitting on the bench. Her face was calm now — the tears had dried, the composure had returned — but something behind her eyes had shifted.
   130|
   131|"Thank you," she said. "For not playing them alone. For bringing them to the room."
   132|
   133|"That is the record," Gabriel said simply. "The record is shared."
   134|
   135|"Yes. It is."
   136|
   137|She stood. She walked to the door. She paused one last time, looking at the whiteboard, at the constitution, at the board that told the truth about the colony's systems.
   138|
   139|"Earth still exists," she said. Not a question. An acknowledgment. A recognition that the world they had left was not extinct, was not destroyed, was not a memory. It was still there, spinning on its axis, rotating around its sun, carrying the people who had sent messages across a quarter billion kilometers of space because the signal was good today and they had wanted to say the things that needed to be said.
   140|
   141|"Yes," Gabriel said. "It still exists."
   142|
   143|She left. He followed, closing the door behind him, the common area empty now except for the hum of the ventilation system and the faint echo of music that lived in the walls.
   144|
   145|---
   146|
   147|Mei was in the greenhouse when the crew session ended. She had chosen to sit out the live session — not because she did not want to hear the messages, but because she had a family message and she wanted to hear it alone, in the place where she spent most of her time, surrounded by the living things she tended and the quiet that only a greenhouse on Mars could provide.
   148|
   149|She listened to her brother's voice on her tablet, sitting on a stool between Row 3 and Row 4 of the growth racks, and she wept quietly while the irrigation system cycled water through the plant trays and the artificial lights cast their steady, warm glow over leaves that had never seen a real sun.
   150|
   151|Her brother had sent a message that was longer than most of the others — twelve minutes of him talking about his farm in central California, about the drought and the soil and the new crop rotation he had implemented and the way the sky looked at harvest time when the dust was high and the light was gold. He was not a man of sentiment. The message was full of data — rainfall figures, soil pH, planting dates — and Mei knew that for him, the data was the sentiment. The numbers were the love.
   152|
   153|When the message ended, she sat for a long time in the greenhouse with the tablet in her lap and the water running in the irrigation lines and the plants breathing the air that the oxygen plant produced, and she thought about the connection between her brother's farm and this greenhouse — two places, two worlds, two people growing things in dirt because that is what humans have always done, in every era, on every continent, on every world they have ever set foot on.
   154|
   155|She stood up. She walked to the seed storage unit at the back of the greenhouse — a climate-controlled case containing the original seed stock that the mission had brought from Earth, most of it already planted, most of it already growing, but a small reserve kept in case of crop failure, contamination, or the need to replace a variety that proved unsuitable for Martian conditions.
   156|
   157|She opened the case and reached past the trays of standard seed — mustard greens, kale, potatoes, soybeans, wheat — to the bottom drawer, where the personal reserves were kept. Seeds that individual crew members had brought from home as part of their personal allotment. A small number of packets, carefully labeled, each one a piece of Earth carried across interplanetary space in a suit pocket or a gear bag or a private kit that the mission planners had allowed because they understood that some cargo could not be quantified in mass or volume.
   158|
   159|Mei pulled out a packet labeled with her own handwriting: *Sunflower. Heirloom variety. Grandmother's garden. Texas. Bring to Mars and try.*
   160|
   161|She had brought the packet because her grandmother had grown sunflowers in a garden behind a house that had been sold, demolished, and replaced by something else before Mei had even landed. The sunflowers had been tall — four, five feet — with dark seeds that her grandmother had dried and saved and replanted every spring for sixty years. Mei had taken a small envelope of the seeds, sealed it, tucked it into her personal kit, and brought it to Mars with no plan and no expectation. Just the idea that maybe, if the conditions were right, she could plant them.

   181|*Gabriel. Before you file the archive entry, I want you to see this.*
   182|
   183|A graph appeared on the screen. Two lines: signal quality over time, and information density per transmission, both plotted across the last two hundred days.
   184|
   185|"What am I looking at?" Gabriel asked.
   186|
   187|*The blue line is signal quality — measured as error-correction recovery rate, scaled from zero to one hundred percent. You can see the improvement over the last seventy-two hours. The blue line is going up. Today's transmission was the highest — ninety-six percent, as you know.*
   188|
   189|"I can see that."

   191|*Now look at the red line.*

High density meant every bit of signal carried useful information. Low density meant the transmission was mostly noise, repetition, or padding.
   194|
   195|"The red line is going down."

   213|"But you don't think it indicates nothing."
   214|

That is — I find this difficult to articulate — both encouraging and concerning.*
