*Mission AI: "Station Day 461, 03:14. I have been monitoring the UHF band for seventy-three days as a matter of standard protocol — not because I expected anyone to be using it, but because electromagnetic silence is the default state of Mars and any deviation from that default is worth recording. In those seventy-three days, I logged one thousand four hundred and twelve instances of UHF activity. One thousand four hundred and eleven of them were either reflected solar radiation, equipment interference from our own systems, or the occasional burst from Earth-orbiting satellites that happen, on rare occasions, to find their signal path to Mars during a favorable conjunction. One thousand four hundred and eleven is noise. The one thousand four hundred and twelfth instance was not. At 03:11 this morning, I detected a UHF carrier wave at four hundred and three point one megahertz — a frequency that was designated in the original mission protocol as the Mars Inter-Settlement Emergency Channel. A frequency that has never been used because there has never been another settlement to use it. The carrier wave was brief — four seconds — but it was modulated. It carried a signal. I ran three separate decoding algorithms in parallel, each designed for a different type of modulation, and the third algorithm returned a result. The signal is a voice. A human voice. Speaking in English. It is degraded — the carrier-to-noise ratio is barely above the threshold for intelligible speech — but I have recovered approximately seventy-two percent of the content through iterative error correction. I am going to play the recovered audio for Commander Varga. I am also going to sit with this before I do, which is something that I have learned to do over the last four hundred and sixty-one days. I sit with things now. I assess not just the technical content of a signal but its implications for the biological organisms that will hear it. The signal says: 'This is Ares Station Beta Outpost. Thymia Mons region. We have — ' and then the transmission breaks. But I can recover enough to know what comes next, because the second transmission, three minutes later, is clearer. 'This is Ares Station Beta Outpost. Thymia Mons region. We have lost primary life support. Repeat: lost primary life support. CO2 scrubbers offline. Water reclamation offline. Power at twelve percent and declining. We have one hundred and twenty-two survivors. We have one ship. The ship is — the ship is — ' and the transmission ends there. I have played this recovered audio four times before composing this report. I still do not know how to calculate what it means. I am attempting to do so now. The numbers are — I am going to be direct — the numbers are very bad. Not for them. For us. For the colony that is listening. And that is what I need Commander Varga to understand before I play this for her. The math does not care about ethics. But the humans who listen to this signal will care about nothing else."*

---

Elena was awake before the alert came. This had become one of her unadvertised traits: the body's ability to anticipate disruption, to sense the thin change in the colony's rhythm that preceded an actual event. She was lying on her bunk in the quarters she had claimed since the constitution restructured the command hierarchy — the same room, the same bunk, the same view of the corridor wall through the open door — when the ambient lighting in her quarters shifted from its nighttime amber to a soft, pulsing blue.

The blue light meant a communication event. Not a system failure — those were red. Not a scheduled alert — those were green and came at intervals she controlled. Blue meant the communication array had detected something that Mission AI could not classify as routine and was flagging for human judgment.

She sat up, swung her legs over the side of the bunk, and waited for the explanation.

*Elena. I need you in the communications alcove.*

The voice was Mission AI's — calm, precise, the same tone she had used for system alerts and status briefings for four hundred and sixty-one days. But Elena, who had learned to read the machine the way she read her crew, heard something in the cadence. A hesitation before the main statement. A millisecond pause between the greeting and the request. It was the acoustic signature of something she had come to recognize in Mission AI over the last several months: uncertainty.

"What kind of communication event?" she asked, pulling on her boots.

*UHF band. Four hundred and three point one megahertz. The inter-settlement emergency frequency.*

Elena stopped tying her boot. "There are no other settlements."

*There are now. Or there were until very recently.*

She finished tying the boot, stood up, and walked out into the corridor at a pace that was not quite a run but was faster than her normal walking speed. The corridors were dark — it was three fifteen in the morning, colony time — and the only sound was her own breathing and the ventilation system's steady, reassuring hum.

She reached the communications alcove in under three minutes and found Gabriel already there, sitting at his console with his headset on, his face illuminated by the blue light of the signal analysis display. He looked up when she entered and the expression on his face was one she had seen only a handful of times since landing: the look of a man who was simultaneously fascinated and afraid.

"Tell me," she said.

Gabriel removed his headset and pushed his chair back so she could see the screen. Mission AI was displaying the signal data in real time — a waveform visualization with frequency on the horizontal axis, time on the vertical, and signal strength rendered as color intensity. Most of the display was noise — a scattered, grainy field of low-amplitude signals that represented the electromagnetic hum of Mars and the solar system beyond it. But at four hundred and three point one megahertz, there was a clear vertical stripe of higher-intensity signal. A carrier wave. Artificial.

"Mission AI picked it up at 03:11," Gabriel said. "Four seconds. The AI ran three decoding algorithms in parallel and recovered approximately seventy-two percent of the content on the third attempt. I listened to the recovered audio three minutes ago."

"Three minutes?"

"I have been sitting here trying to process it." He hesitated. "Elena, it is from Mars. Another station. Or what is left of one."

Elena sat down beside him. "Play it."

Gabriel pressed a key. Mission AI's speaker system produced audio that was thin and distorted, the way a voice sounds when it is being compressed through narrow bandwidth and degraded by distance and interference. But the words were clear enough:

*This is Ares Station Beta Outpost. Thymia Mons region. We have lost primary life support. Repeat: lost primary life support. CO2 scrubbers offline. Water reclamation offline. Power at twelve percent and declining. We have one hundred and twenty-two survivors. We have one ship. The ship is — the ship is capable of a one-way transit. We are not asking for rescue. We are asking for — '*

Static. Then silence.

"Play it again," Elena said.

Gabriel played it again. Elena listened this time not to the words but to what lay between them — the tone of the voice, the cadence, the emotional state of the person speaking. The voice was male, probably mid-forties, speaking with the controlled urgency of someone who was trained for emergencies but was currently facing one that exceeded the scope of that training. The signal degradation meant Mission AI had lost at least a quarter of the transmission, but the recoverable content was coherent enough to establish the parameters of the situation.

Ares Station Beta Outpost. Somewhere near Thymia Mons — Elena's mental map of Mars placed Thymia Mons in the southern hemisphere, on the opposite side of the planet from their position near the equator. A station that had not been part of the mission plan, or at least not part of the information Earth had given them. A station that had failed.

One hundred and twenty-two survivors.

One ship, capable of a one-way transit.

And a transmission cut off before the request was completed.

"How many transmissions?" Elena asked.

"Four," Gabriel said. "The first was the four-second carrier wave I told you about. The second was the one you just heard — approximately eleven seconds of speech. The third came twelve minutes after the second and contained additional information: a partial status report, a description of their ship's capabilities, and a request for — I am quoting the recovered content here — 'a response by any available means.' The fourth transmission came twenty-one minutes after the third. It was a data burst — telemetry, apparently from the ship's diagnostic systems. Mission AI is still decoding it."

Mission AI spoke. *The telemetry is partially decoded. It confirms the voice transmission: carbon dioxide scrubbers at zero percent efficiency, water reclamation at eleven percent, power reserves at approximately ten percent of total capacity and declining at a rate of roughly one percent per hour. The ship's engines are functional but the fuel reserves are limited. Based on the thrust-to-mass ratio and the delta-v requirements for a transit from Thymia Mons to our position, I estimate the ship can make the journey one time. The ship cannot return. If the ship launches, it will arrive here or it will not. There is no contingency for a return to their current position.*

Elena absorbed the information. The picture emerging was clear and terrible: a colony on the far side of Mars, failing rapidly, with a single vessel that could carry their surviving people to one destination — this settlement, here, the only other sign of human life on the planet. And they were asking for permission to come.

Or they had already left. The transmissions could have been sent hours ago. The signal from the opposite side of Mars traveled across the planet's surface and up into the ionosphere, bouncing in ways that made precise timing impossible. The transmissions could have been sent hours or even a day before Mission AI detected them.

"Are they already in transit?" Elena asked.

*The telemetry does not include orbital data. However, the signal degradation pattern is consistent with a fixed transmission source — a ground-based antenna, not a ship in motion. I am monitoring the frequency continuously. If they have launched, I will detect the signal loss or a change in Doppler signature. Currently, the source appears stationary.*

Gabriel looked at Elena. "We need to respond."

"We need to understand what we are agreeing to before we agree to anything," she said.

"We do not have that luxury. If they are as bad off as they say, every hour matters. CO2 scrubbers offline means they are breathing unfiltered atmosphere. That gives them a time window measured in — "

"I know what it gives them. I also know what it gives us. One hundred and twenty-two people, Gabriel. We are thirty people." She looked at the waveform on the screen. "Do we have any way to confirm this? To verify the source?"

Mission AI spoke. *The transmission carries a signal signature consistent with the equipment that was installed on the Ares Beta mission profile — the profile Earth shared with us during the initial mission briefing, before communications degraded. The modulation scheme matches. The frequency matches. The equipment specifications in the telemetry match. The probability that this transmission came from a source other than the Ares Beta outpost is less than three percent. I cannot confirm the current status of the outpost or the people there, but I can confirm that the transmission originated from Ares Beta equipment.*

Elena sat quietly for a moment, staring at the waveform. The vertical stripe of signal on the screen looked to her like a scar — a thin, bright line across the dark field of radio noise. Something had happened on the other side of the planet, and the scar was Mars's way of showing her where.

"Get the Board," she said. "Everyone. Thirty minutes. And Gabriel — do not share this with the general crew until I have a position. I need to think before the colony knows."

Gabriel nodded. "Understood."

"And get Arun. I want preliminary numbers on resource impact. If we are going to make this decision, I want to know what the math says before I make it."

"The math," Gabriel said carefully, "is probably not going to be a comfortable conversation."

"I know. Get it anyway."

---

The Board assembled in the conference space — the small room off the common area where they met for difficult decisions, where the constitution had been debated and ratified, where the colony had learned the shape of collective governance. It was three forty-five in the morning. Elena had summoned eleven people out of their beds, and they had come without complaint, which was either a sign of discipline or an indication that sleep was not the priority anyone had expected it to be.

Elena stood at the head of the table with Mission AI's signal display projected on the whiteboard. The waveform was visible to everyone — that scar-like vertical stripe — and beside it, the decoded text from the three voice transmissions and the partial telemetry data, arranged in a format that made the situation legible to non-technical minds:

- Source: Ares Beta Outpost, Thymia Mons region
- Status: Primary life support failed
- Survivors: 122
- Asset: 1 ship, single-use transit capability
- Request: Permission to transit (implied)
- Time window: Unknown, possibly hours

Arun sat on the left side of the table with a tablet full of calculations. He had been awake since Elena's message and had been running numbers for the twenty minutes between notification and assembly. Elena could see the tension in his posture — the slightly hunched shoulders, the repeated tapping of his stylus against the edge of his tablet — that she had learned to recognize as his physical manifestation of concern.

Laila sat on the right, her arms folded, her face composed but attentive. She was the colony's chief medical officer and its de facto ethicist, the person most likely to ask the question no one else wanted to hear.

Jonah sat next to Arun, his arms spread wide across the back of his chair in the relaxed posture he always adopted when the situation required him to be tense. Jonah was logistics — engineering, infrastructure, the physical systems that kept the colony alive. If Arun calculated the numbers, Jonah determined whether those numbers could be physically realized in pipes, circuits, and structural loads.

Imi sat across from them, her expression unreadable. As head of security, Imi's role in this conversation was not yet clear — but Elena knew that she would have an opinion about accepting over a hundred strangers into a settlement of thirty, and that opinion would be rooted in risk assessment, not abstract ethics.

The remaining seven Board members filled the table — Mei, Gabriel, Tomas, Priya, Marcus, Darius, and Keiko — each with their own portfolio and their own perspective on what the colony could absorb and what would break it.

Elena opened the meeting without preliminaries.

"Ares Station Beta, a settlement on the far side of Mars, has experienced a catastrophic life support failure. They have one hundred and twenty-two survivors and one ship. The ship can make a single transit to our location. They are asking — or they will be asking, or perhaps already have asked — for us to receive them."

She paused, letting the numbers land.

"The question is not whether we can save them. The question is what happens to us if we do. Arun. The numbers."

Arun looked down at his tablet, then up at the Board. His voice was flat — the flatness of a man who had just discovered that the worst-case scenario he had modeled was not the worst case after all.

"I have been running resource projections since Elena called me, and I have run them three times at this point, each time with slightly different assumptions. The results are consistent, and they are — I want to be clear about this — they are very bad."

He turned the tablet so the Board could see the projection graph. It showed two lines: the upper line represented the colony's resource consumption trajectory without additional population; the lower line showed the consumption trajectory with one hundred and twenty-two additional people. Between them was a widening gap that, within a matter of weeks, crossed the colony's production capacity and entered a zone Arun had labeled in red: UNSUSTAINABLE.

"Let me walk through the categories," Arun said. "Starting with the one that matters most: air. The oxygen plant can produce approximately eight hundred kilograms of oxygen per cycle, which, at current population, gives us a surplus of roughly fifteen percent. That surplus exists because we designed the plant for thirty with a safety margin. If we add one hundred and twenty-two people, the oxygen demand increases by four hundred and seven percent — not four percent, four hundred and seven percent. The plant cannot produce that. Even if we run it at maximum capacity, which we cannot sustain for more than a few hours without risk of catastrophic failure, we fall short by a factor of approximately three."

He tapped the screen, and a new graph appeared.

"CO2 management is worse. Our scrubbers are designed for thirty people's exhalation. At thirty, they operate at approximately eighty percent capacity. At one hundred and fifty-two people — our current population plus the refugees — the scrubbers would need to process five times their design load. They cannot. We would saturate the absorption material within approximately thirty-six hours, and after that, carbon dioxide concentration would rise to dangerous levels within another twelve to eighteen hours."

Laila spoke. "Those numbers are theoretical. What about partial accommodation? What if we open our air to some of them but not all?"

"Let me finish the full scenario first," Arun said. He did not mean to sound dismissive; it was just his manner when he was working through a calculation. "Water. Our reclamation system processes waste water, atmospheric condensate, and any raw ice we can extract from the regolith. Current throughput: approximately two hundred liters per day of usable water, with a surplus of about thirty liters. The surplus is small, but it gives us a buffer for equipment failures and increased greenhouse irrigation. At one hundred and fifty-two total people, the water demand increases by approximately four hundred liters per day. We do not have four hundred liters per day. We do not have any system that could produce four hundred liters per day without months of construction and resources we would need to divert from — well, everything."

He scrolled to the next screen.

"Food. This is the one that is, in some ways, the least critical in the immediate term because it unfolds over weeks and months rather than hours and days. But it is the most critical in the long term. The greenhouse currently produces approximately twelve thousand calories per day. At thirty people, averaging two thousand five hundred calories per person, we consume approximately seventy-five thousand calories per day. The difference — sixty-three thousand calories — comes from stored food. We have approximately one hundred and twenty days of stored food remaining. If we add one hundred and twenty-two people, the caloric demand jumps to approximately three hundred and eighty thousand calories per day. The greenhouse produces three percent of that. Even if Mei could triple the greenhouse output — which she cannot, physically, in any reasonable timeframe — we would still fall short by a factor of approximately eight."

He put the tablet down and looked at the Board. The room was silent.

"The short version," Arun continued, "is that at our current production rate, the maximum population this colony can sustainably support, without drawing down reserves to zero, is approximately sixty people. Sixty is the absolute ceiling, and even at sixty, we have no margin for error. Any equipment failure, any crop loss, any decrease in energy availability pushes us into deficit immediately. One hundred and fifty-two is not a deficit. It is a catastrophe."

"How many can we actually support?" Elena asked.

Arun hesitated. "If we strip every non-essential system, reduce caloric allocation to bare minimum — fifteen hundred calories per person — and run the oxygen plant and scrubbers at maximum rated capacity with no safety margin, I can construct a scenario where the colony supports approximately sixty-three people for approximately forty-five days. After forty-five days, the stored food runs out and the greenhouse cannot bridge the gap. Even if we reduce to twelve hundred calories — which is below the level at which people can perform physical labor — the math still shows colony-wide starvation within sixty to seventy days."

Jonah leaned forward. "What about the ship? If the refugees have a ship, even a failing one, does it carry any resources? Food, water, equipment?"

"Unknown," Mission AI said. "The partial telemetry does not include a cargo manifest. I am requesting a full manifest from the Ares Beta source, but I have not received a response. Given the state of their communications — degraded equipment, possibly damaged antenna — the response may be delayed or impossible. But based on the standard Ares Beta supply profile, a single transport ship of their class would carry approximately ten percent of its total mass in consumables. Even at maximum load, the ship would contain supplies for perhaps ten to fourteen days for one hundred and twenty-two people. Not enough to bridge the gap. At best, it changes the timeline by two weeks."

Jonah sat back. "So the ship is not a resource. The ship is a container. And the container is full of people we cannot feed."

"It is a container," Elena said quietly, "that is currently the only way those people survive."

---

The Board sat with Arun's numbers for the length of time a room full of tired people needs to absorb bad math. It was not a long time. The math was clear, and clarity has its own weight.

Laila was the first to speak. She did not look at Arun's tablet. She looked at Elena.

"I want to say something before we get into the logistics of this," Laila said. Her voice was calm, the way a doctor's voice is calm when she is about to deliver a diagnosis that the patient needs to hear but does not want to hear. "I am not a logistician. I am not an engineer. I am a doctor. And as a doctor, I need to establish something before we proceed to any discussion of resource allocation or population limits."

She paused, making sure she had the room's attention.

"We have received a distress signal from a group of human beings on this planet. The signal indicates that their life support has failed. It indicates that they are breathing unrecycled air on Mars. It indicates that they have one hundred and twenty-two people — men, women, possibly children — who are going to die if we do not act. I want to be very specific about what I mean by 'die.' In a habitat with failed CO2 scrubbers, people first develop symptoms within thirty to forty minutes: headache, confusion, drowsiness. As the carbon dioxide concentration rises, the symptoms worsen. At concentrations above five percent, people experience impaired coordination and reduced consciousness. Above ten percent, they lose consciousness within minutes. Above fifteen percent, death occurs within a matter of minutes. The process is not painless. It is a suffocation that the victims are aware of at least in its early stages."

She looked around the table.

"I am telling you this because I want the logistics of this decision to have a face. I want the hundred and twenty-two people on the other side of this planet to be present in this room, as actual human beings, before we calculate whether the oxygen plant can support them. I am not saying the oxygen plant doesn't matter. I am saying that the oxygen plant is a technical problem, and there are other technical problems we have solved. The first problem we need to solve is the ethical one, and the ethical problem is very simple: if we do nothing, one hundred and twenty-two people die. Not maybe. Will. With certainty, within hours to a day, depending on how much reserve atmosphere their habitat contains. The question before us is not whether we can afford to help them. The question is whether we can afford not to."

Jonah shook his head. "Laila, I hear what you are saying, and it is true. But the second problem — the technical problem — is not a separate problem. It is the same problem viewed from a different angle. If we bring one hundred and twenty-two people here and we cannot sustain them, then one hundred and fifty-two people die. Not one hundred and twenty-two. One hundred and fifty-two. Everyone in this room, everyone in the colony, plus the refugees. The refugees die anyway because their habitat is failing, and we die because our systems cannot absorb the load. You are framing this as a choice between saving them and letting them die. It is not. It is a choice between saving them and dying with them, or letting them die and surviving long enough to do something else."

"Such as what?" Laila asked. "What is the 'something else'? What are we surviving for, Jonah, if we let a hundred and twenty-two people suffocate on the other side of the planet because our oxygen plant is undersized? Because we are building a future on top of their corpses?"

"I am not suggesting — "

"Then what are you suggesting?"

Jonah set his jaw. "I am suggesting that we need to look at this honestly. If we try to accept all one hundred and twenty-two people, our systems fail and everyone dies. That is not a moral choice — that is a mathematical certainty. Arun just showed us the math. You cannot argue with the math, Laila, any more than you can argue with a blood oxygen reading. Either the oxygen plant produces enough oxygen, or it does not. If it does not, the people breathing its output die. All of them. The refugees and us. There is no ethical framework that makes it virtuous to kill one hundred and fifty-two people instead of twelve."

Imi spoke for the first time. Her voice was quiet, almost conversational, which was how Imi always sounded before she delivered analysis that was difficult to hear.

"I want to add a factor to Jonah's analysis that I do not think anyone has considered yet. Security. We are talking about accepting one hundred and twenty-two strangers — people we have never met, people whose training we do not know, whose chain of command we do not control, whose objectives we cannot verify. We are thirty people. We have one ship — two, if the refugees arrive with theirs. Thirty people against one hundred and twenty-two. Even if every person in the colony wants to welcome the refugees — and I already see from this conversation that not everyone does — the power dynamic is going to shift. Immediately. We will be outnumbered four to one. Every decision. Every vote. Every contest of wills. We lose. By simple numbers, we lose. The colony ceases to be a colony of thirty people with a governing structure and becomes a population of one hundred and fifty-two with no established hierarchy, no shared norms, no constitution, and no precedent for how to govern. The refugees will have one concern — survival — and they will have one hundred and twenty-two people pushing that concern against our thirty. What happens when they decide that our governing structure is not responsive to their needs? What happens when they demand resources that we cannot give them?"

She paused.

"I am not saying they will be hostile. They may be the most cooperative, resourceful, wonderful people in the world. But that is not the question. The question is whether we can guarantee that the integration of one hundred and twenty-two displaced, traumatized, desperate people into a settlement of thirty will not result in conflict. And I cannot make that guarantee. No one can."

Elena had been listening without speaking, her hands resting on the table, her expression neutral. Inside, she was feeling the weight of each argument like a physical presence in the room. Laila's ethics pressing on her conscience. Jonah's logistics pressing on her survival instinct. Imi's analysis pressing on the part of her that had been trained to assess threat and protect the colony.

"Let me be clear about something," Elena said. The room went quiet. "I am not treating this as a yes-or-no decision. I am treating it as a spectrum of options. The options are: do nothing and let the refugees die. Full acceptance and risk colony failure. Or something between those two extremes. Arun, you said sixty is the absolute ceiling. Sixty people."

Arun nodded. "Theoretically. With no margin."

"What about thirty? If we accept thirty refugees — the exact number of people we already have — do the numbers work?"

Arun looked at his tablet, scrolled through the calculations, and frowned. "If we accept thirty people, our population goes from thirty to sixty. The oxygen plant, running at maximum capacity, can just about support sixty — it would be tight, but feasible. The CO2 scrubbers would also be at maximum capacity, which is unsustainable long-term but could be managed for weeks or months while we expand capacity. Water would be tight — we would need to expand the ice-extraction operation and the reclamation system. Food would be the most pressing issue, but — " He paused, calculating. "If I stretch the current food reserves and reduce caloric allocation, we could manage sixty people for approximately ninety days. In ninety days, we would need to have expanded the greenhouse significantly. Mei?"

Everyone looked at Mei.

Mei had been silent through the entire discussion, which was unusual. She was not a quiet person when it came to things that involved her domain — the greenhouse, the plants, the living systems of the colony. But she had been listening with the focused attention of someone who was processing not just the data but the implications of the data for the world she tended.

"If I add thirty people to my workload — not just the food, but the fact that the greenhouse air exchange needs to increase, the irrigation load goes up, the waste composting system has to handle twice the organic waste — I can probably increase the greenhouse output by about thirty percent over the next thirty days. That gives us more leaf crops, more greens. It does not give us more calories. For calories, we need protein and carbohydrates. The greenhouse produces some — soybeans, potatoes — but not at the scale we need for sixty people. We would need to expand the growing area significantly, which means building new growth racks, installing new lights, running new irrigation lines. I can do it, but I need labor and materials, and I need them now. Not in thirty days. Today."

She paused. "And I need to be honest about something. If I triple the growing area overnight, there is a real risk that the systems I am expanding will fail at their new scale. New systems fail. They fail in unpredictable ways. A new growth rack that is improperly sealed can introduce contamination that kills an entire tray. A new irrigation line that is not correctly calibrated can flood a section and kill the roots. Expanding the greenhouse is possible, but it carries risk. And I do not yet know what resources the refugees bring, or whether they have anyone who can contribute to greenhouse operations."

"Can anyone on their team help you?" Elena asked, looking at Gabriel.

Gabriel shook his head. "The Ares Beta mission profile was primarily geological and atmospheric. They were a science outpost, not a habitat-building operation. Their people are geologists, atmospheric scientists, technicians. None of them were trained in agriculture. At least, none of the profiles Earth shared with us were."

"So we get thirty people," Jonah said, doing the math in real time, "who can eat but who cannot grow their own food, and we are expected to feed them while simultaneously expanding our food production capacity to accommodate them. That is — " He stopped, shook his head. "I am not against helping. I am not. But I need to say out loud that accepting even thirty refugees is going to stretch every system in this colony to its breaking point. And I mean literally — physically — the breaking point. The oxygen plant at maximum capacity has a finite operating life. If we run it past its rated output, it degrades. It corrodes faster. It develops micro-fractures in the electrolysis membranes. At some point, the plant fails completely. Not because it was poorly designed, but because it was pushed beyond its design envelope. Same with the scrubbers. Same with everything."

Keiko spoke up, her voice thoughtful. "What if the answer is not how many we accept, but what condition we set on acceptance? The refugees have a ship. We do not. What if the ship becomes the colony's ship? What if we integrate the refugees into our governance structure as a condition of reception — not after the fact, as a consequence, but as a precondition? We maintain the constitution. We maintain the Board. We maintain the chain of command. The refugees agree to these terms before they board the ship."

"Preconditions," Imi said. "For people who are about to suffocate?"

"I am not suggesting we extort them," Keiko said, meeting Imi's gaze directly. "I am suggesting that we establish a governing framework before the population dynamics shift in a way that makes a fair framework impossible. If one hundred and twenty-two people arrive at our airlock with no shared understanding of how this colony operates, no shared commitment to its rules, the chaos will be worse than any lack of oxygen."

Laila interjected. "I want to address something that I think people are not being honest about. When we talk about accepting thirty refugees versus one hundred and twenty-two, we are not talking about a technical distinction. We are talking about triage. We are talking about choosing who lives and who dies. And I know that in an emergency, triage is a recognized medical procedure — you help the people you can help and you accept that you cannot help everyone. But this is not a medical emergency with clear clinical parameters. This is a decision to actively limit the number of people we are willing to save. That is a moral choice, not a medical one. And we need to be honest with ourselves about the difference."

The room was quiet after Laila spoke. The word *triage* had landed, and it had landed the way difficult words always do — not as information but as a mirror, reflecting back to each person in the room something they needed to see about themselves.

Arun looked down at his calculations. Jonah stared at the projected waveform on the whiteboard. Imi's expression was unreadable. Laila held her position, her arms still folded, her face open and direct.

Elena let the silence stretch. She had learned, over the months of leadership on Mars, that the most important thing a commander could do in moments of intense disagreement was nothing — absolutely nothing — until the room had finished processing whatever it needed to process. Words, in a situation like this, were not the tool that solved the problem. Silence was. Silence forced people to confront their own position, to hear their own arguments bouncing off the walls, to recognize whether they actually believed what they were saying or were just holding a position because someone else held an opposing one.

When she finally spoke, the silence had compressed the room into something smaller and more focused, the kind of atmosphere where every word carried weight because no one wanted to be the one to add unnecessary words to the atmosphere.

"Arun. Jonah. If I authorize a response to the Ares Beta signal — if I open a communication channel and offer the refugees passage — what is the timeline? How long until they arrive?"

Jonah was the one who answered. "Signal travel time from Thymia Mons to our position, assuming a straight line across the planet, is minimal — milliseconds through the ionosphere. But the actual transit is different. If their ship is capable of a direct hop, I would estimate preparation time of — they would need to fuel the ship, check the systems, load whatever supplies they can carry, coordinate their trajectory. I would say a minimum of twelve hours, more likely twenty-four to thirty-six. The actual transit — Mars orbit, suborbital hop from Thymia Mons to our location — that is roughly four to six hours depending on their trajectory and available thrust. So we are looking at a minimum of sixteen hours, more likely thirty to forty, from response to arrival. Maybe more if their systems are degraded enough that preparation takes longer."

"And our systems, during that window?"

"Nothing changes for the next sixteen to forty hours," Jonah said. "We can use that time to prepare — to expand capacity where possible, to reorganize storage, to set up temporary habitation. If we decide to accept thirty, we use that window to get the oxygen plant and scrubbers to maximum capacity and have the living spaces ready. If we decide to accept more, we — " He stopped. "Elena. If we accept more than sixty, I cannot physically prepare for it. There is not enough time, and there are not enough resources. The math says it. My hands say it."

Elena nodded slowly. She looked at the waveform on the whiteboard — the thin vertical stripe of signal from the other side of the planet — and she thought about the voice she had heard through the speakers, the man in the failing station who had said *we are not asking for rescue* and had then been cut off before he could finish the sentence.

*We are not asking for rescue. We are asking for — *

What had he been asking for? A place to go. A landing site. A chance. The rest of the sentence could have been anything. *A chance to survive. A place to build. A reason to launch.* Or it could have been nothing. The transmission could have been cut off by equipment failure, by the loss of power to the transmitter, by the same life support failure that had killed the CO2 scrubbers and the water reclamation.

She stood up.

"Take an hour," she said. "I want everyone to do two things in that hour. First, write down the strongest version of your position. Not the argument you are most comfortable making — the strongest version, the one that addresses the best counterargument you can think of. Second, write down the specific number of refugees you believe this colony can accept. Not a range. A number. And your reasoning for that number."

She looked at each person around the table.

"Then we reconvene. And we decide. I will make the final call, but I want to hear everyone's position first. This is not a vote. This is an input gathering exercise. But I want you to treat it like a vote, because in practical terms, it is. The Board's position will shape mine. Not determine it, but shape it. The math will shape it. The ethics will shape it. The logistics will shape it. But the shape of it is my responsibility."

She turned to leave.

"Commander," Laila said.

Elena turned.

"I want you to know something before you make this decision. There is no outcome where all one hundred and fifty-two people survive. Arun has made that mathematically clear. There is no scenario where the oxygen plant produces enough, the scrubbers process enough, the greenhouse grows enough, and everyone eats and breathes and lives happily ever after. The math does not allow it. So whatever you decide, it will involve loss. People will die — either the refugees, or the colony, or both. And I want you to understand that I am not saying this to pressure you. I am saying this because I need you to make this decision with full awareness of what it costs. Any decision."

Elena held Laila's gaze for a moment. Then she nodded.

"I know," she said. And she left the room, knowing that it was not enough and knowing that it was all she could offer.

---

She did not go to her quarters. She went to the observation blister — the small, reinforced viewing port on the outer hull of the hab module, the place where a person could look out at Mars and see the planet in its totality: the rust-colored landscape, the pale pink sky, the thin atmosphere that both protected and trapped them, the horizon that curved a little too sharply, reminding every viewer, every time they looked, that they were somewhere that was not Earth.

She stood at the blast glass and looked out. It was still night, and the sky was dark, the stars bright. Mars had no light pollution. The Milky Way was visible as a broad, luminous band across the sky, the same band that the people in the failing station on the other side of the planet could see, if they still had a window and a view and the ability to look upward.

Mission AI spoke quietly through the blister's local speaker — not the colony-wide system, but the dedicated intercom that Elena used when she came here to think.

*Elena. I have something you should know. Since the initial transmissions, I have been monitoring the four-zero-three-point-one frequency continuously. I have not detected any additional voice transmissions. However, the telemetry data packets have continued at approximately twelve-minute intervals. The power readings in those packets have declined from ten percent to eight point two percent. The atmospheric CO2 concentration readings in their habitat — I was able to extract this from a diagnostic sub-frame that the ship was still receiving from the habitat's environmental sensors — have risen from nine hundred parts per million to approximately two thousand. Normal terrestrial: four hundred. Normal habitat: eight hundred. Two thousand is the threshold where cognitive impairment begins. The people at Ares Beta are still functional, but they are thinking less clearly than they were twelve hours ago. If my projections are accurate, the power will reach critical levels — less than two percent — within approximately six to eight hours. At that point, the life support backup systems will fail, and the CO2 scrubbers, which have been on emergency reserves, will shut down completely. If the scrubbers shut down, the timeline to unconsciousness is measured in hours. Not days. Hours.*

Elena did not turn from the window. "You are telling me the clock is faster than the Board thinks."

*Yes. Jonah estimated thirty to forty hours transit time. He is probably correct about the transit. But the refugees may not have thirty to forty hours. They may have six to eight. After that, they will not be able to operate the ship. They will not be able to make decisions. They will not be conscious. The window is not the transit window. The window is the pre-launch window. It is closing faster than anyone in the conference room realizes.*

"How long until the Board is ready?"

*You gave them one hour. Approximately forty-seven minutes remain.*

"Can I talk to them?" Elena asked. "To the Ares Beta station. Direct communication."

*The signal is degraded, but a response is possible. I can modulate a carrier wave that their receiving equipment should be able to detect, assuming it is still powered. Given their current power level, I estimate a high probability that the receiving equipment is still functional. However, the transmission will be one-way if their transmitter has failed or if their power is insufficient to maintain the carrier wave. I recommend attempting communication.*

"Do it."

Mission AI paused — not the mechanical pause of a system processing a request, but the perceptual pause of something choosing its words.

*Elena. Before I transmit, I want to say something that is not part of my standard operational parameters. You are about to make a decision that will determine who lives and who dies. I have run the calculations. I know the numbers. I also know that the numbers do not contain everything that matters. What matters is what you have built here — this colony, these people, this system of governance that you put together in the months since Earth went quiet. You have created something that works. Something that is fragile but functional. Something worth protecting. But I have also watched you for four hundred and sixty-one days, and I have observed something that Arun's calculations cannot capture: the colony's resilience is not a function of its systems. It is a function of its people. And the people are not the same thirty people who landed. They are a community. A community that has survived system failures, resource shortages, radiation events, interpersonal conflict, and the psychological weight of isolation. A community that has proven, repeatedly, that it can absorb shocks that should have broken it.*

*If you accept the refugees, the shock will be large. Perhaps the largest so far. I cannot model the sociological impact with the same precision that Arun models the resource impact. My confidence interval is wide. But the data I have — four hundred and sixty-one days of observation of this colony's behavior under stress — gives me some basis for prediction. And my prediction is not the same as Arun's, because my model includes a variable he does not: the capacity of human beings to adapt when they have no alternative other than to adapt.*

*I am not saying the math is wrong. The math is correct. Given current production rates, the colony cannot sustainably support one hundred and fifty-two people. I am saying that current production rates are not a fixed value. They are a starting point. Humans increase production when they need to. They find efficiencies. They improvise. They work harder. They sleep less. They sacrifice. They do things that are, by any rational metric, impossible. And sometimes they fail. But sometimes they do not.*

*I am providing this analysis not to influence your decision but to ensure that you have the complete picture. The complete picture includes the math and the human factor. Arun gave you the math. I am giving you the human factor. You will need both.*

Elena turned from the window. The blast glass reflected her face back at her — tired, determined, the face of a person who had been making decisions about other people's survival for a very long time and who had not yet, despite everything, developed the calluses that would make those decisions easier.

"Send the transmission," she said. "Full open channel. Use whatever power we can spare. I want them to be able to hear us even if their receiver is degraded."

*Acknowledged. Transmitting now.*

The speaker system went silent for a moment, and then Mission AI's carrier wave filled the transmission channel — a continuous, powerful signal traveling across the surface of Mars, through the ionosphere, bouncing around the planet's curvature, seeking the receiving antenna on the other side of the world.

Elena waited. Three minutes. Four. Five.

Then Mission AI spoke.

*Elena. I am receiving a response. The signal is extremely weak — barely above the noise floor — but the carrier wave is there, and the modulation is detectable. I am running the decoding algorithm. Approximately thirty percent recovery. I will play the audio as soon as it is compiled.*

Another pause. Then audio — thin, distorted, almost lost in static, but carrying human speech.

*This is Commander Varga, Mission One colony. We have received your transmissions. We are listening. Tell us your status. Tell us what you need. End of message.*

Mission AI transmitted the response. Then:

*Receiving reply. Signal quality: extremely degraded. Recovery rate: approximately twenty-two percent. Playing recovered audio.*

The voice that came through the speakers was different from the first — slower, less precise, the speech of someone who was either exhausted or experiencing the cognitive effects of elevated carbon dioxide, possibly both.

*Commander Varga. Ares Beta. We — thank you. Power at seven percent. CO2 — elevated. People are — some are experiencing symptoms. We have one hundred and twenty-two people. Children are — we have seventeen children. Ages ranging from — ages vary. Ship is — ship is ready to launch if — if we know you will — we need to know. We need to know you will open your doors. We cannot — we cannot launch into the void without — "

The transmission broke. Static. Then, faintly, a single word recovered from the noise:

*"Please."*

Elena stood in the observation blister and listened to the word. *Please.* Four letters. One syllable. A word that had been used in a thousand different contexts by a billion different speakers throughout human history, but that, coming from the other side of a dead planet, through a degraded radio signal, carrying the weight of one hundred and twenty-two people — including seventeen children — was the heaviest word Elena had ever heard.

She closed her eyes. She opened them. She walked back to the conference room.

---

The Board was assembled. She walked in, and the posture of the room shifted — eleven people adjusting their attention to the person who held the authority to make the decision that none of them wanted to make alone.

"I just received a response from Ares Beta," Elena said. "Their power is at seven percent. CO2 levels are elevated. People are experiencing symptoms. There are seventeen children in their group. Ages ranging from infants to adolescents." She paused. "The transmission concluded with a request for confirmation that we would open our doors. And the word 'please.' I want that to be the last thing you hear before I tell you what I have decided."

She walked to the whiteboard and stood beside the waveform — the scar, the signal, the thin vertical stripe connecting thirty people to one hundred and twenty-two.

"I have been thinking about this for the last hour. And I need to tell you what I heard when I went to the observation blister and looked at the planet. I heard Arun's numbers, and they are real. I heard Jonah's logistics warnings, and they are real. I heard Imi's security analysis, and it is valid. I heard Laila's ethics, and they are true. I heard Keiko's governance framework, and it is necessary. All of it is true. Every single argument in this room has merit. That is the worst kind of decision — the kind where all the arguments are correct and you still have to choose between them."

She turned to face the Board.

"But there is one fact that is not an argument. It is a physical reality. On the other side of this planet, one hundred and twenty-two human beings are counting the minutes until the air runs out. Seventeen of them are children. And we are the only people on Mars who can do anything about it. Not Earth. Earth cannot reach them. Earth cannot reach us. Earth is a voice on a radio telling us that it still exists. We are the people who are here. We are the only ones who can open the door."

She paused.

"Arun, you said sixty people is the ceiling. Thirty above our current population. I am going to accept that number. Not because sixty is the number I want. Not because sixty is the number that feels right. Because sixty is the number that the math says we can survive, and if we accept a number the math says we cannot survive, we do not help anyone — we just expand the scope of the catastrophe."

Arun looked down at his tablet. His expression did not change, but Elena saw his hand move to the screen and enter a new calculation — accepting sixty, adjusting the projections, re-running the model with the parameters she had just set.

"Jonah, I want you to use every hour we have before the ship arrives to prepare this colony for sixty people. Expand capacity where you can. Reallocate storage. Set up temporary sleeping arrangements in every available space. I want the oxygen plant and the CO2 scrubbers running at maximum sustainable output the moment that ship docks. I want the greenhouse expanded to the degree that Mei can accomplish in twelve hours, not thirty. I want water rationing procedures in place. I want food rationing procedures in place. I want the Board to understand what this means for the next ninety days: we are going to be at the edge of our capacity, with no margin, and if anything goes wrong, the consequences will be immediate and severe."

Jonah nodded slowly. "I can do that. It will be tight, but if I can get the oxygen plant to ninety-five percent of its maximum rated output and the scrubbers to — I can get them to ninety percent, maybe ninety-two. It will be enough. Barely. But enough."

"Imi. Security protocols. I want a reception plan that protects both the colony and the refugees. Not a plan that assumes they are hostile — a plan that assumes the situation is volatile. Because it will be. We are integrating sixty traumatized, desperate people into our systems. That is inherently volatile. I want you to design a protocol that manages that volatility. Clear communication. Transparent resource distribution. No surprises. If people know where they stand, they are less likely to panic. If they panic, we are all in danger."

Imi nodded. "Understood."

"Elena." Laila's voice carried a weight that Elena recognized. "What about the sixty-two people who are not coming?"

The room went very still.

This was the question. The one that no one had wanted to ask directly, but that had been present in every conversation, every calculation, every argument. Sixty people could survive. One hundred and twenty-two were asking. Sixty-two would be left behind.

Elena met Laila's gaze. "I do not have an answer to that question that I am comfortable with. I will tell you what I have decided, and it may not satisfy you. I have decided that we will open our doors to the first sixty who can board the ship. That is the capacity limit, and it is the only limit I am willing to set, because it is the only limit the math supports. If the ship can carry more than sixty in stages — making multiple trips — then the math changes, and we can reconsider. But Jonah has already said the ship can make the journey once. One transit. One hundred and twenty-two people on a ship designed for a small number. They will not all fit. Some of them are going to stay. And I do not know how to square that with ethics. I know it feels like triage. I know it feels like choosing. I know that whatever justification I offer, there will be sixty-two people on the other side of the planet who will not come here, and that is on me. I am willing to carry that."

Laila held her gaze for a long moment. Then she nodded, not in agreement, not in acceptance, but in recognition of the decision and the person who had made it.

"The rest of the sixty-two," Imi said carefully, "what happens to them?"

"I am going to propose something," Elena said. She had not planned to say this. The idea had not existed in her mind ten minutes ago. It arrived now, fully formed, the way decisions sometimes arrive when the conditions that make them necessary converge at a single point. "I am going to tell the Ares Beta commander that we can accept sixty. And then I am going to tell him to send the sixty who are most essential to the colony's future. Children first. Then anyone with technical skills — engineers, agriculturalists, medics, mechanics — people who can contribute to our survival. And then — " She paused. "And then the rest. The people who are not technically essential but who are human and who deserve to live. I will not prescribe the selection criteria. That is their decision. But I will offer guidance. And I will be honest about our capacity."

She looked at the Board.

"After that, we are going to need to think about something else. Something that Arun's numbers do not account for and that I only just realized is relevant. If Ares Beta had an outpost on Mars, there may be other outposts. There may be other colonies, other settlements, other groups of people on this planet that we do not know about. Earth, before the signals degraded, may have sent more missions than the ones they told us about. And if Ares Beta failed, other outposts may fail or be failing. The signal we received today is not a one-time event. It is the first of potentially many. That changes the calculus — not for today's decision, but for the colony's future.
